summary: The note argues that a revival of ethnobotanical heritage, meaning the use of native plants and herbs, is reshaping regional cuisine. It draws on interviews with chefs, an agricultural expert and an herbalist to cover flavor, sustainable farming, medicinal value, global exchange, culinary education and institutions. It concludes that this is a lasting movement linking cultural identity, sustainability and health.
one_line: Native plants and herbs are driving a lasting revival of regional cuisine that ties together heritage, sustainability, health and education.
key_facts: Chef Elena Martinez of the farm restaurant La Tierra Prometida was interviewed on September 15, 2023 about native plants and herbs in culinary traditions.
Martinez said "People are rediscovering the depth and complexity that native ingredients bring to our tables."
Chef John O'Connell of The Wild Thyme Bistro in rural Vermont cites ramps, juniper berries and sumac as wild plants used by forebears.
By October 12, 2023, The Wild Thyme Bistro will have introduced an event dedicated solely to foraged herbs and native plants.
Agricultural expert Dr. Sophie Zhang, interviewed October 28, 2023, said native species are adapted to local climate and require less water and pesticides.
Herbalist Jane Parker, interviewed November 6, 2023, said ginseng, turmeric and ginger carry medicinal properties recognized for centuries.
Michelin-starred Chef André Gauthier spoke on December 5, 2023, likening native ingredients in his dishes to telling a story.
Martinez is also a culinary instructor at the Cozumel Cooking School, teaching local chili varieties, hoja santa and native fruits.
The Culinary Museum of Heritage Plants in Boston, Massachusetts has exhibits on historical and modern uses of native plants in American cooking.
Wild rosemary in Mediterranean dishes and epazote in Mexican cuisine are given as examples of native plants defining regional flavor.
Restaurants and suppliers increasingly label ingredients with the farm of origin, traditional uses and environmental benefits.
The note calls the interest in native plants "not a fleeting trend but a burgeoning movement."
